To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the United Kingdom's social-security system is not well modeled by a social-security system, that the system is solvent, that the incentives created by the system match well with the behavior of older persons, and that this behavior is not well modeled as a social-security system.

the United Kingdom has a large private-pension system and that the incentives created by the state pension and disability-benefit systems are consistent with the observed labor-market behavior of men in the United Kingdom.

the incentives created by the structure of the United Kingdom's state pension system match well with the labor-market behavior in the data, and that the incentives facing older workers are similar for those with private pensions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two questions: first, why do people retire from the labor force? and second, what is the role of the social-security pension system in this process?
the labor-market behavior and the coverage of social-security systems of older persons in a country where the social-security system is not the dominant source of income for most pensioners.
the incentives created by the structure of state and private pensions and their effect on labor-market behavior of those close to retirement age.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the United Kingdom's labor-force participation rate of the elderly is lower than that of most other countries.
the United Kingdom has a relatively low level of retirement, with the majority of people continuing to work beyond the age at which the state pension is available.
there has been an increase in the proportion of older people who are not working, but that this increase has been concentrated in the male population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the United Kingdom's labor market for older people is characterized by a high rate of early retirement among men, a high rate of labor-force participation among women, a high level of disability benefits, and a low level of unemployment among older workers.
the labor market participation of men in the 55 and over age group is very low, and that of women is rising, but from a very low base.
the United Kingdom has a relatively generous and efficient system of social insurance, which provides a good safety net for those who have worked but who cannot afford to retire.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, despite the fact that state pension benefits are relatively generous, they do not appear to create a strong incentive for early retirement.

the incentives created by the pension system are consistent with the observed labor-market behavior of men and women in the United Kingdom, and that the system is not a major contributor to the observed decline in labor-market participation among men.

, while the incentives facing workers in the United Kingdom are not particularly favorable to continued labor-market participation, they are not so adverse that the labor-market participation of older workers is likely to be a serious policy issue.
